title: Hilda and the Polka-Dot Berries
markdown:
High up in the far green peaks of Bramblehorn, where clouds played hide-and-seek with jagged rocks, lived Hilda. Not a grumpy ogre. Her laugh tumbled like pebbles downhill, heart as bright as a sunbeam. Skin the colour of warm earth, small horns curling like little crescent moons.

She loved a good competition. The best in all Bramblehorn was the annual Berry Bonanza: a wide sun-drenched meadow, sweet scent of ripe brambleberries, the biggest juiciest berry before anyone else. Grand prize: a gleaming Golden Acorn, much bragging and admiration.

“Are you ready, Hilda?” Grumble, so fuzzy and grey he looked like a misplaced piece of mountain mist, long floppy ears twitching like furry radar. Oldest friend, quiet and steady.

“Ready as I’ll ever be.” She bounced on sturdy boots. Beside Grumble, Scree, a tiny marmot with a remarkably keen nose and a tail that seemed to have a mind of its own, squeaked and did a dizzying dance. Twitching whiskers. Boundless energy.

“This year I’m winning for sure. The Golden Acorn is mine.” She pictured it on her mantelpiece, catching the light.

With a cheerful wave to villagers gathering at the meadow’s edge, baskets ready, they set off toward the whispering woods. Crisp air, pine needles, damp earth. Sunlight dappled, dancing patterns. Hilda skipped, eyes scanning every bush, heart thrumming.

“Look, Grumble. A plump one.” A berry seemed to wink from beneath a broad green leaf.

Grumble squinted. “A bit small for a champion. It lacks a certain gravitas.”

Scree scampered up a moss-covered rock. Squeaks that meant: keep looking, the best is yet to come.

Hilda’s competitive spirit was a strong steady flame. A fizzing in her tummy. The part she loved best: exploration, discovery, the cusp of something wonderful. She hurried deeper, sure the best berries hid off the beaten path.

Ancient oaks, gnarled branches like wise old fingers. Ferns tickling her knees. Quieter woods, unseen birds, soft crunch of boots. Then a peculiar sound, like a kettle boiling very slowly, and a voice crackly as dry leaves.

“Oh dear. This is most vexing. Utterly, utterly vexing.”

Hilda pushed aside a curtain of thick emerald ivy. A small sun-dappled clearing. A witch, hat a bit lopsided, like a toadstool that had seen better days, stirring a bubbling pot with a long gnarled spoon. Beside her, grooming with supreme importance, a sleek black cat with eyes like polished emeralds.

“Hello?” Softer now. The woods had a way of making one feel small.

The witch jumped, nearly dropping her spoon. “Mercy me. A young ogre. You startled me. I’m Morwen. And this is Flicker, my most discerning companion.”

Flicker, without looking up from paw-licking, gave a slow blink. “Mrow.” Hilda suspected it meant: do try not to drip on the rug.

“I’m Hilda. And these are Grumble and Scree.” Grumble rumbled. Scree, peeking from behind a leg, gave a tiny brave squeak.

“We have a rather peculiar problem. Take a look at our berries.”

Hilda blinked. The berries, which should have been plump and ruby-red, were covered in bright bold polka-dots: red, blue, yellow, haphazard, like a picture book gone haywire.

“They used to be perfectly ordinary. Plump and sweet, ideal for a good old-fashioned berry pie. Now they look like a jester’s dropped laundry.”

Flicker let out a long meeeow: utterly undignified. And frankly quite undigestible.

Hilda giggled. “They look funny.”

“Funny indeed. But not very tasty. And I was hoping for a nice berry pie this evening.”

Hilda’s mind raced. A competition, a peculiar problem, a witch and her cat. Much more interesting than the biggest berry. “How did this happen?”

Morwen wrung her hands. “We suspect that clumsy gnome inventor, Pipkin. Hollow log by the Whispering Falls. Always tinkering with his Sparkle Dust. He claims it makes things sparkle.”

Hilda knew of him: wobbly inventions, a tendency to trip, a remarkable talent for misplacing his spectacles. He usually supplied the Sparkle Dust for the Bonanza, meant to make berries gleam, not wear ridiculous polka-dots.

“Pipkin needs his spectacles,” Grumble rumbled, ears drooping. A gnome without glasses was like a bird without wings.

Scree darted forward, tiny determined paw toward the deeper woods. Squeaks: let’s go.

And so they set off, Morwen and Flicker trotting elegantly, toward the Whispering Falls. Air cooler. The murmur of the falls became a louder song. Trees taller, branches entwined like an ancient tapestry, sunlight a soft green glow.

They found Pipkin in a terrible tizzy. Small, beard like a bird’s nest that had seen better days, very flustered. “My Sparkle Dust. Gone all dotty. And my spectacles. I can’t find them anywhere. Oh, the calamity.”

He clutched a singed pouch pulsing with unnatural multi-coloured light. Hilda peered inside: tiny iridescent particles. “This is the Sparkle Dust. And Pipkin can’t see properly. That’s why he made the mistake.”

Sometimes problems are not as tricky as they seem. A few different pairs of eyes. A willingness to look closely.

“Where did you last see your spectacles?”

“Adjusting the Sparkle Dust near the big mossy rock. Then I tripped on a root, and… they just vanished.”

Grumble listened. “I hear rustling. Not the wind. Something skittering.”

Scree scampered toward the ferns, nose twitching. Squeaks: under the big wobbly mushroom. A glint.

There they were. Nestled among tangled roots of a giant wobbly mushroom, glinting in dappled sunlight: Pipkin’s spectacles, round, shiny coppery metal.

He put them on with a gasp. The world snapped into crisp focus. “Thank you. Thank you, everyone.” He peered at the dust. “A little too much moonbeam essence, perhaps. And a whisper of dragon’s breath.”

With steady hands he added a tiny pinch from another vial, clear liquid smelling of honeysuckle. The dust became a soft gentle sparkle, like dancing fireflies. He sprinkled a little over a nearby leaf. No polka-dots. Morning dew catching first sun.

Hilda’s smile crinkled the corners of her small horns. The funny berries seemed a distant silly memory. Someone else would take the Golden Acorn, and that was all right. She had helped set a pouch right, and that sat better than any prize on a mantelpiece. Grumble’s ears, which had drooped for Pipkin, stood up again. Scree did one last dizzying dance, this time for spectacles rather than berries.

Morwen rustled a happy cackle. Flicker purred and rubbed Pipkin’s leg. As the sun dipped, orange and purple on the peaks, they walked back toward the meadow. Hilda carried no prize. She carried a corrected pouch, a gnome who could see, and friends who knew how to listen for rustling that was not the wind. The meadow, when they reached it, was still having a Bonanza. She did not mind missing the shout.
characters: Hilda (young ogre who loves a good competition), Grumble (a fuzzy grey friend with floppy ears)
